questions.question: You test whether a mean equals a stated value, σ is unknown, and n = 16. Which test and df do you use?
questions.explanation: σ is unknown, so use the t-test. df = n − 1 = 15.

questions.question: The one-sample t statistic is...
questions.explanation: t = (x̄ − μ₀) ÷ (s/√n): the distance of the sample mean from the claim, measured in estimated standard errors.

questions.question: n = 16, x̄ = 76, s = 8, H₀: μ = 72 (right-tailed). What are t and the decision at α = 0.05 (critical value 1.753)?
The 95% CI for a mean is (47.9, 56.1). A two-tailed test at α = 0.05 of H₀: μ = 50 would...
questions.explanation: 50 lies inside the interval, so the test fails to reject. A two-tailed α-test rejects μ₀ exactly when μ₀ is outside the (1 − α) CI.

questions.question: For a statistic of 2.2, why is the p-value from the z curve smaller than from the t curve when n = 5?
options: t curves have fatter tails, so extreme values are less surprising
t uses α instead of p
questions.explanation: Heavier tails mean values like 2.2 occur more often under the t curve, so the tail area (p-value) is larger. Using z would overstate the evidence.

questions.question: A t-test on n = 7 data points contains one extreme outlier. What should you do?
options: Look at the data, as the t-test is sensitive to outliers in small samples
questions.explanation: The t-test assumes roughly normal data. With a tiny sample, one outlier can distort x̄ and s. Inspect the data and consider a robust or nonparametric alternative.
